overview: The Nara period gave Japan its first permanent capital, Heijo-kyo, laid out on the grid of the Tang capital Chang'an. The court ran the country under the ritsuryo codes, made Buddhism a state religion and compiled its first histories and poetry.

items.text: The Manyoshu, an anthology of 4,516 poems by emperors, courtiers and frontier guards, was compiled; its latest dated poem is from 759.
The Kojiki, and in 720 the Nihon Shoki, recorded the myths and early history of the imperial line.
The Great Buddha of Todaiji, a bronze figure about 15 meters high, was dedicated in a ceremony attended by monks from India and China.
Emperor Shomu ordered a state temple and nunnery in every province.
The ritsuryo codes, the Taiho of 701 and the Yoro of 718, organized government, taxes and land on Tang models.
Confucian learning was taught at the state academy to train officials.
Chinese characters were used for all government records, and census and tax registers were kept on paper.
Trunk roads with post stations linked the capital to the provinces.
The Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara were listed by UNESCO.
The Manyoshu remains the foundation of Japanese poetry.

fall.text: Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, in 794, the start of the Heian period.

sources.title: UNESCO, Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara
